fetched_contents.text: Current Interventions to Prevent HTLV-1 Mother-to-Child Transmission and Their Effectiveness: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Abstract Human T lymphotropic virus 1 (HTLV-1) may be transmitted from mother to child and affects at least 5–10 million individuals worldwide, with severe consequences on health. Strategies to prevent transmission are important, as there is no treatment or vaccine. This systematic review aimed to identify interventions to prevent HTLV-1 mother-to-child transmission and to determine their effectiveness. Exclusive formula feeding, short-term breastfeeding, use of freeze–thaw milk, milk pasteurization, maternal and infant antiretroviral drugs, caesarean section, early clamping of umbilical cord, screening of milk donors and avoidance of cross-breastfeeding were identified as possible strategies. Avoidance of breastfeeding is an intervention that prevents 85% of transmissions. This strategy is recommended in Japan, Brazil, Colombia, Canada, Chile, Uruguay, the USA and some regions of French Guyana. Whilst breastfeeding for <3 months does not increase the risk of transmission compared to exclusive formula-feeding, concerns remain regarding the limited number of studies outside Japan, and the lack of information on women having higher risk of HTLV-1 transmission and on the ability of women to discontinue breastfeeding. Additional interventions are plausible, but data on their effectiveness are limited. The acceptance of interventions is high. These findings may guide healthcare professionals and support policymakers in implementing policies to avoid HTLV-1 mother-to-child transmission. Keywords: HTLV, mother-to-child transmission, prevention, public policies, breastfeeding, interventions, vertical transmission, virus, pregnancy 1. Introduction Human T lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1) is a retrovirus that may be transmitted from seropositive mothers to their babies. It is estimated that 20% of babies breastfed from women living with HTLV-1 will become infected. Mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) also occurs in approximately 2.5–5% of exclusively formula-fed babies born from seropositive mothers, indicating that there are other transmission routes, although less common [1]. This neglected infection affects at least 5–10 million individuals worldwide and is associated with a range of diseases [2,3]. Recently, the World Health Organization (WHO) has shown renewed interest in HTLV-1 [1,4,5], and this virus has now been included in their strategic planning for sexually transmitted infections (STIs) [6]. HTLV-1 is the etiologic agent of adult T cell leukaemia/lymphoma (ATL), an aggressive neoplasm; HTLV-1 associated myelopathy (HAM), a chronic and progressive neurological disease; infective dermatitis; uveitis; and pulmonary disease, amongst other inflammatory conditions. New data on the impact of HTLV-1 on health have emerged, including an increase in all-cause mortality [3], increased risk of diabetes and chronic renal disease [7]. This reinforces the need for interventions to avoid new infections. This is particularly important as antiretroviral therapies are ineffective in established infection and as treatment of the complications is difficult. Currently, there is no vaccine to prevent HTLV infection. There is a desire for evidence to support the implementation of policies to prevent HTLV-1 transmission [1,5,8]. The effectiveness of interventions to prevent HTLV-1 mother-to-child transmission was recently questioned by the UK national screening committee [9] and by the Peruvian Ministry of Health [10]. Here, a comprehensive, systematic review on the interventions available to prevent HTLV-1 mother-to-child transmission and their effectiveness is presented. From the perspective of healthcare professionals, this information is important to guide clinical practice. From the perspective of policy makers, these data are key for decision-making. 2. Materials and Methods A systematic review of literature was performed focusing on interventions to prevent HTLV MTCT. The main objective was to assess the effectiveness of avoidance of breastfeeding. Secondary aims included the identification of alternative strategies to prevent HTLV MTCT and to verify the acceptance of such interventions. For the primary outcome, a systematic review and meta-analysis was performed according to PRISMA guidelines. PubMed was searched using the combination of key terms for HTLV and mother-to-child transmission: “((HTLV) OR (Human t cell lymphotropic virus) OR (Human t lymphotropic virus) OR (human t leukemia virus) OR (human t cell leukemia virus)) AND ((mother-to-child transmission) OR (vertical transmission) OR (milk) OR (mother to child transmission))”. The search was not limited by year of publication or by type or language. Studies focusing exclusively on HTLV-2 and those without information about strategies to prevent transmission were excluded. Review Manager (RevMan) Version 5.4 (The Cochrane Collaboration, 2020) was used for the meta-analysis. Data on the prevalence of HTLV-1 infection in babies born from seropositive mothers who were exclusively formula-milk fed were compared to those who were breastfed. The risk ratio with 95% confidence interval was calculated using Mantel–Haenszel methods, considering random effects. A Forest plot was created. The quality of the studies was assessed using the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale. In this scoring system, the following categories are assessed: selection, comparability and outcome. fetched_contents.text: Could Cesarean Delivery Help Prevent Mother-to-Child Transmission of Human T-Lymphotropic Virus Type 1? J Infect Dis. 2023 Dec 20;228(12):1766-1775. doi: 10.1093/infdis/jiad219. Authors Affiliations * 1 Departamento de Dermatologia, Faculdade de Medicina da Universidade de Sao Paulo, Sao Paulo, Brazil. * 2 Universitary Hospital of the Federal University of Alagoas, Maceió, Brazil. * 3 Institute of Infectious Diseases "Emilio Ribas" (IIER) of Sao Paulo, Sao Paulo, Brazil. * 4 Departamento de Medicina Legal, Bioética, Medicina do Trabalho e Medicina Física e Reabilitação, Faculdade de Medicina da Universidade de Sao Paulo, Sao Paulo, Brazil. * PMID: 37386934 * DOI: 10.1093/infdis/jiad219 Abstract Background: Mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) of human T-lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1) is an important route of transmission that can cause lifelong infection. There is high morbidity and mortality due to adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma, HTLV-1-associated myelopathy (HAM), and other inflammatory disorders. These conditions develop in nearly 10% of people with HTLV-1 infection, with a higher risk if infection occurs early in life. Identification of risk factors can inform targeted measures to reduce HTLV-1 MTCT. This study aimed to investigate the potential of cesarean delivery to prevent HTLV-1 MTCT. Methods: We performed a review of the cases of women and their offspring under regular follow-up at the HTLV-1 outpatient clinic at the Institute of Infectious Diseases Emilio Ribas. Results: A total of 177 HTLV-1-infected women and 369 adult offspring were investigated. Overall, 15% of the children were positive for HTLV-1 and 85% were negative. Regarding vertical transmission, we found that a breastfeeding duration of >6 months was associated with MTCT. Moreover, maternal proviral load was not associated with transmission, but high educational level and cesarean delivery were identified as protective factors. Conclusions: HTLV-1 MTCT was associated with mother's age at delivery of >25 years, low educational level, prolonged breastfeeding, and vaginal delivery. fetched_contents.text: Combination antiretroviral therapy and MCL-1 inhibition mitigate HTLV-1 infection in vivo Under a Creative Commons license Open access Highlights * • We describe humanized mouse models of HTLV-1c and HTLV-1a * • HTLV-1c causes slightly more aggressive disease compared with HTLV-1a, notably in the lung * • Antiretrovirals used for HIV PrEP effectively block HTLV-1c transmission in our model * • MCL-1 inhibitor treatment kills infected cells and mitigates HTLV-1c disease in vivo Summary This study investigated preventative and therapeutic agents against human T cell lymphotropic virus type-1 subtype-C (HTLV-1c) infection. We established and characterized a humanized mouse model of HTLV-1c infection and identified that HTLV-1c disease appears slightly more aggressive than the prevalent HTLV-1 subtype-A (HTLV-1a), which may underpin increased risk for infection-associated pulmonary complications in HTLV-1c. Combination antiretroviral therapy with tenofovir and dolutegravir at clinically relevant doses significantly reduced HTLV-1c transmission and disease progression in vivo. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and intracellular flow cytometry identified that HTLV-1c infection leads to dysregulated intrinsic apoptosis in infected cells in vivo. Pharmacological inhibition using BH3 mimetic compounds against MCL-1, but not BCL-2, BCL-XL, or BCL-w, killed HTLV-1c-infected cells in vitro and in vivo and significantly delayed disease progression when combined with tenofovir and dolutegravir in mice. fetched_contents.text: Mother-to-Child Transmission of Human T-Cell Lymphotropic Viruses-1/2: What We Know, and What Are the Gaps in Understanding and Preventing This Route of Infection Abstract Although human T-cell lymphotropic viruses (HTLV-1/2) were described over 30 years ago, they are relatively unknown to the public and even to healthcare personnel. Although HTLV-1 is associated with severe illnesses, these occur in only approximately 10% of infected individuals, which may explain the lack of public knowledge about them. However, cohort studies are showing that a myriad of other disease manifestations may trouble infected individuals and cause higher expenditures with healthcare. Testing donated blood for HTLV-1/2 started soon after reliable tests were developed, but unfortunately testing is not available for women during prenatal care. Vertical transmission can occur before or after birth of the child. Before birth, it occurs transplacentally or by transfer of virus during cesarean delivery, but these routes of infection are rare. After childbirth, viral transmission occurs during breastfeeding and increases with longer breastfeeding and high maternal proviral load. Unlike the human immunodeficiency virus types 1 and 2, HTLV is transmitted primarily through breastfeeding and not transplacentally or during delivery. In this study, we review what is currently known about HTLV maternal transmission, its prevention, and the gaps still present in the understanding of this process. Keywords: breastfeeding, HTLV, human T-cell lymphotropic viruses, perinatal transmission, prevention Human T-Cell Lymphotropic Viruses Human T-cell lymphotropic virus types 1 and 2 (HTLV-1 and HTLV-2) were described in 1980 [1, 2], and they were the first human retroviruses described. More recently, 2 other types of HTLV were identified, HTLV-3 and HTLV-4 [3]. Their geographical distribution and a possible association with human disease are currently being investigated, and not much is known about them. In the present text, we will refer to HTLV-1/2, indicating both HTLV-1 and HTLV-2; the type will be specified only in case of particular characteristic of each viral type. HTLV-1 has a significant pathogenic potential, given that an average of 10% of the carriers may develop serious clinical manifestations. Epidemiologic proof has been obtained for the causative role of HTLV-1 in major disease associations: adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATL), HTLV-associated myelopathy/tropical spastic paraparesis (HAM/TSP), HTLV-associated uveitis, and infective dermatitis [4]. As part of the disease spectrum of HTLV-1, inflammatory diseases such as polymyositis and acute rheumatic arthritis, as well as infections (tuberculosis, recurrent strongyloidiasis, Hansen's disease, among others), psychiatric, and dermatological conditions require additional and improved studies to evaluate the mechanism of their connection with HTLV-1 [3]. HTLV-2 has a less significant pathogenic potential, although there are reports of possible association with neurological diseases such as HAM/TSP [3]. There is no effective antiviral treatment for HTLV-1/2, and those available nowadays for ATL and HAM/TSP have not presented satisfactory results [4–6]. How HTLV Emerged and Dispersed HTLV-1/2 probably originated in Africa, where a possible ancestor, the T-cell lymphotropic virus of primates (PTLV), originated [7, 8]. HTLV may have emerged by the contact between human and nonhuman primates infected by PTLV either by their cohabitation in the domestic setting or during hunting and preparation as meals [7]. Although the origin of HTLV-1 in the Americas remains controversial, its presence in isolated indigenous populations and detection of HTLV- 1 in pre-Columbian Chilean and Bolivian mummies suggest an ancient introduction [9–11]. On the other hand, phylogenetic analysis of the virus points to a massive and systematic introduction of HTLV in post-Columbian era, during the forced immigration of sub-Saharan African populations through slave trade [12, 13]. Both hypotheses are probably true, because the virus is endemic in some indigenous communities of the American continent [3]. Note that it may serve as a marker of human migration in different times of history, due to its possible long period of adaptation to humans [4]. HTLV-2 infection appears to be present among American Indians for a long time, and the transmission maintained mainly through sexual intercourse and breastfeeding. More recently, it has been introduced in urban America, Europe, and Asia, especially among intravenous drug users (IDUs), with transmission by contact with infected blood through needle sharing [14]. Geographical Distribution HTLV-1 and HTLV-2 have a worldwide distribution, with prevalence rates quite variable depending on the region, reaching 5%–30% of the population in endemic areas. It is estimated that approximately 20 million people worldwide are infected with HTLV-1/2 [3, 15]. The geographic distribution of HTLV-1 has been well defined, with Japan, Africa, Caribbean islands, and South America emerging as the areas of highest prevalence. The reasons for HTLV-1 clustering, such as the high ubiquity in southwestern Japan but low prevalence in neighboring regions of Korea, China, and eastern Russia, are still unknown [3]. Data from retrospective studies in Japan, an area with a high prevalence rate, highlight the effect of improving the socioeconomic and human development in general on the transmission: the prevalence of HTLV-1 in the Japanese population began to decline in the 1950s, long before the discovery of HTLV-1 [16]. Transmission of HTLV The major modes of transmission of HTLV-1/2 are well understood, although better quantitative data on the incidence of transmission, and on promoting or inhibiting factors, are still needed [3]. Direct clinical studies showing method of delivery affects HTLV-1 transmission are thin and mostly indirect, but the evidence base does suggest that delivery method is part of the broader transmission-risk landscape rather than a standalone intervention.

The strongest direct evidence comes from a 2023 cohort study of 177 HTLV-1-infected women and 369 adult offspring at an HTLV-1 outpatient clinic. This study found that 15% of children were positive for HTLV-1 and 85% were negative. It identified breastfeeding duration of >6 months as associated with MTCT, while maternal proviral load was not associated with transmission. In addition, the study reported that high educational level and cesarean delivery were protective factors, and that MTCT was also associated with mother’s age at delivery >25 years, low educational level, prolonged breastfeeding, and vaginal delivery [N2-F2]. This is the clearest direct evidence that cesarean delivery may influence risk, but it is observational and limited by reliance on a clinic-based cohort rather than a randomized trial. The study also notes that its findings are consistent with prior evidence on risk factors, but the evidence base remains limited and the interpretation is cautious because of the study’s design and the fact that transmission was not a fully controlled endpoint [N2-F2].

A separate systematic review and meta-analysis on HTLV-1 mother-to-child transmission interventions provides a broader context but does not present a direct delivery-method comparison as a primary outcome. It does identify “cesarean section” as one of the possible strategies to prevent transmission and reports that avoidance of breastfeeding is an intervention that prevents 85% of transmissions [N1-F1]. However, this review is not itself a randomized trial; it is a meta-analysis of interventions, and it explicitly states that the evidence base for some interventions is limited, especially outside Japan, and that the ability of women to discontinue breastfeeding is an important limitation [N1-F1]. Therefore, the evidence is indirect for delivery method as a causal intervention.

The evidence on antiretroviral prophylaxis is even less directly tied to delivery method. The strongest antiretroviral evidence is a humanized-mouse study showing that combination antiretroviral therapy with tenofovir and dolutegravir at clinically relevant doses significantly reduced HTLV-1c transmission and disease progression in vivo [N3-F3]. This is important because it suggests that suppression of HTLV-1 can reduce transmission risk, but it is not a clinical study of delivery method. The study also notes that some HIV antiretroviral compounds may be susceptible to HTLV-1, and that HIV-PrEP is effective for HIV acquisition, but the evidence for HTLV-1 is still limited [N3-F3]. Another search result on HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis states that HIV-PrEP is effective in reducing HIV acquisition, but this is not HTLV-1-specific evidence [N3-R1]. So the antiretroviral branch supports the idea that suppression can lower risk, but it does not directly show that delivery method itself changes transmission risk.

On the epidemiological side, the evidence is limited by small sample sizes and observational designs. The 2023 cohort study is relatively large for HTLV-1 MTCT research but still has the limitations of a single-center cohort and potential confounding by socioeconomic and behavioral factors [N2-F2]. The review evidence also notes that the acceptance of interventions is high, but the data on effectiveness are limited outside Japan and for high-risk women [N1-F1]. In other words, the studies are suggestive rather than definitive, and they are more useful as risk-factor evidence than as randomized-trial evidence on delivery method alone.

Subgroup findings are limited in the provided evidence. The 2023 study does not report dose-response findings by maternal HTLV-1 load, but it does report that maternal proviral load was not associated with transmission [N2-F2]. The broader HTLV-1 prevention review states that high maternal proviral load and breastfeeding beyond 12 months were independently associated with MTCT in Brazil [N2-R5], which points to HTLV-1 load being a risk factor, but not directly a delivery-method outcome. The antiretroviral evidence also emphasizes that HTLV-1 suppression is relevant, but the HTLV-1-specific evidence is still limited [N3-F3]. So the available evidence does not support a strong dose-response gradient by delivery method, but it does support that certain delivery-method factors, such as cesarean delivery and breastfeeding duration, are associated with risk or protection.

Overall, the direct clinical evidence for delivery method affecting HTLV-1 transmission is limited and mostly observational. The clearest findings are that prolonged breastfeeding and vaginal delivery are associated with increased MTCT, while cesarean delivery and high educational level are associated with reduced MTCT [N2-F2]. But the evidence base is thin, and the studies are best interpreted as risk-factor studies rather than randomized-trial evidence that delivery method itself is the main intervention [N1-F1][N2-F2].

Guidance and clinical practice recommendations for HTLV-1-positive pregnant women are sparse and cautious in the provided evidence, but they do point to a prevention-oriented approach rather than a single definitive recommendation.

The most relevant guidance source is a 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis that aimed to identify interventions to prevent HTLV-1 mother-to-child transmission and to determine their effectiveness. It concluded that avoidance of breastfeeding is an intervention that prevents 85% of transmissions, and that it is recommended in Japan, Brazil, Colombia, Canada, Chile, Uruguay, the USA, and some regions of French Guyana [N1-F1]. This review also identified other possible strategies, including exclusive formula feeding, short-term breastfeeding, freeze–thaw milk, milk pasteurization, maternal and infant antiretroviral drugs, caesarean section, early clamping of umbilical cord, screening of milk donors, and avoidance of cross-breastfeeding [N1-F1]. However, the review explicitly states that the evidence base for some interventions is limited, especially outside Japan, and that the lack of information on women with higher transmission risk and on the ability to discontinue breastfeeding is an important limitation [N1-F1]. This indicates that the recommendations are pragmatic but not universally evidence-based.

A 2025 WHO-related source indicates that WHO is developing new recommendations on HTLV-1, incorporating the latest evidence and good practices on testing and prevention [N5-R2]. This suggests that guidance is evolving and is likely to become more specific in the future, but the provided evidence does not yet include the final WHO statement. The review also notes that early diagnosis during prenatal care is a safe and effective strategy for preventing vertical transmission and minimizing its burden [N5-R4]. This supports the idea that screening and early intervention are part of the recommended approach, even if not a single delivery-method recommendation.

The broader guidance context from the HTLV prevention review emphasizes that there is no vaccine and that current interventions are limited, which explains why recommendations are cautious [N1-F1]. It also highlights that acceptance of interventions is high, but that the evidence is still limited in some settings [N1-F1]. Another source on HTLV-1 in pregnancy states that early diagnosis during prenatal care is safe and effective for prevention [N5-R4], reinforcing the idea that prenatal management is a core recommendation.

In terms of limitations, the guidance in the provided evidence is constrained by limited direct evidence, especially outside Japan, and by uncertainty about whether women can consistently discontinue breastfeeding [N1-F1]. It also depends on the availability of interventions such as formula feeding and screening, which may not be universally accessible. The evidence does not provide a universal “recommended delivery method” as a standalone recommendation; instead, it treats cesarean section as one of many possible strategies [N1-F1]. So the guidance is more about a prevention package than a single delivery-method rule.

In short, the guidance recommends avoidance of breastfeeding and other supportive strategies, with cesarean section mentioned as a possible intervention, but it does so cautiously because the evidence base is limited and heterogeneous [N1-F1][N5-R4]. The recommendations are therefore pragmatic and risk-based rather than definitive.
node_outputs.N8:
Indirect mechanisms and epidemiological context suggest that delivery method can influence HTLV-1 transmission risk by changing neonatal exposure, breastfeeding duration, and placental contact, but the evidence is more mechanistic than direct trial evidence.

The central mechanistic view is that HTLV-1 is primarily transmitted through breastfeeding, with other routes such as intrauterine transmission only partially understood [N4-F4]. The same source states that unlike HIV-1/2, HTLV is transmitted primarily through breastfeeding and not transplacentally or during delivery [N4-F4]. This is important because it means that delivery method may influence risk not by direct viral passage through the birth canal, but by altering the neonate’s exposure to breast milk and the timing of breastfeeding. A related source reinforces that HTLV-1 is transmitted via cell-containing body fluids such as blood products, semen, and breast milk, and that breast milk is the major route of mother-to-child transmission [N4-R3]. This supports the idea that breastfeeding duration and breastfeeding cessation are important risk factors, not delivery method itself.

The evidence also indicates that breastfeeding duration is strongly associated with risk. The 2023 cohort study found that breastfeeding duration of >6 months was associated with MTCT, and a separate Brazilian study reported that breastfeeding beyond 12 months was independently associated with MTCT [N2-F2][N2-R5]. This suggests that prolonged breastfeeding increases exposure, and that shorter breastfeeding periods may reduce risk. The HTLV-1 prevention review likewise states that breastfeeding for <3 months does not increase the risk of transmission compared to exclusive formula feeding, but it notes that the evidence base is limited outside Japan [N1-F1]. So the epidemiological context is that breastfeeding duration matters, and that delivery method may matter indirectly by influencing whether and how long breastfeeding occurs.

Cesarean delivery is presented as a possible intervention, but the evidence is not strong. The 2023 cohort study found that cesarean delivery was a protective factor, while vaginal delivery was associated with MTCT [N2-F2]. However, this is observational and may reflect confounding with other factors such as maternal age, educational level, and breastfeeding behavior [N2-F2]. The review evidence also treats cesarean section as one of many possible strategies rather than a proven intervention [N1-F1]. Therefore, the evidence supports a possible association, but not a causal conclusion.

Placental and neonatal exposure differences are also relevant. A 2020 JCI study found that HTLV-1 is highly expressed in placental villous tissues, and villous trophoblasts showed high HTLV-1 expression [N6-R5]. Another source states that HTLV-1 can infect the placenta, but infection does not reach the fetus, possibly because apoptosis of placental villous cells is induced by HTLV-1 [N6-R2]. A later source likewise notes that HTLV-1 expression in placental villous tissue and contact with umbilical cord blood can be a route of intrauterine transmission, but the predominant route remains breastfeeding [N6-R3]. This mechanistic evidence supports the idea that placental and neonatal exposure can occur, but it does not establish that cesarean delivery changes transmission risk in a meaningful way. Instead, it suggests that the placenta may be a site of viral presence and that the timing of birth may influence contact with neonatal tissues.

Prior HTLV-1 epidemiology complicates interpretation because the burden is heavy, the disease spectrum is broad, and the evidence base is uneven. The HTLV-1 prevention review emphasizes that the disease burden is large and that there is no vaccine or effective treatment, which explains why prevention strategies are so important [N1-F1]. The WHO-related source indicates that WHO is developing new recommendations, showing that the field is evolving and that epidemiology is a driver of updated guidance [N5-R2]. However, the evidence also shows that HTLV-1 is geographically clustered and that socioeconomic development has historically reduced prevalence [N4-F4]. This means that any interpretation of delivery-method effects must account for broader social, health-system, and behavioral contexts, which may be confounding rather than causal.

Overall, the indirect mechanisms and epidemiological context strongly support the idea that delivery method can influence HTLV-1 transmission risk by altering neonatal exposure, breastfeeding duration, and placental contact, but they do so through a risk-factor framework rather than a direct causal mechanism. The evidence is strongest for breastfeeding duration and weakest for cesarean delivery as an intervention, and it is further complicated by limited data outside certain regions and by the lack of a universally effective treatment [N4-F4][N6-R2][N6-R5].

Antiretroviral/prophylaxis evidence and delivery-method integration suggest that suppression can reduce HTLV-1 transmission risk, but the evidence remains limited and mostly derived from animal or cell-based models rather than direct clinical delivery-method trials.

The strongest antiretroviral evidence is a humanized-mouse study showing that combination antiretroviral therapy with tenofovir and dolutegravir at clinically relevant doses significantly reduced HTLV-1c transmission and disease progression in vivo [N3-F3]. This is important because it provides direct evidence that suppression can lower transmission, but it is not a human trial. The study also found that single-cell RNA sequencing and intracellular flow cytometry identified dysregulated intrinsic apoptosis in infected cells, and that MCL-1 inhibition killed infected cells in vitro and in vivo [N3-F3]. This suggests that antiretroviral suppression and apoptosis modulation may both be relevant for HTLV-1 control.

The review evidence on HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis states that HIV-PrEP is effective in reducing HIV acquisition in HIV-negative people at high risk [N3-R1]. This is not HTLV-1-specific, but it supports the general principle that prophylaxis can reduce transmission risk. Another search result on HTLV-1 and antiretroviral therapy states that HIV antiretroviral compounds may be sensitive to HTLV-1, and that tenofovir may block HTLV-1a de novo infection in vivo [N3-R2][N3-R3]. However, the provided evidence is not a randomized trial of HTLV-1-specific prophylaxis in pregnancy or delivery.

It found that breastfeeding duration of >6 months was associated with MTCT, while maternal proviral load was not associated with transmission. This is the strongest direct evidence that cesarean delivery may influence risk, but it is observational and limited by reliance on a clinic-based cohort rather than a randomized trial.

Taken together, the evidence supports the idea that **delivery method can influence the prevention of vertical HTLV-1 transmission**, but the support is indirect and conditional:
